requirements.requirement: Limit traffic from node2 toward node3 to 1 Mbit/s
requirements.summary: VyOS qos policy shaper LIMIT-NODE2-TO-NODE3 (bandwidth 1mbit) was configured and bound as egress on eth2 (facing node3) via cmd-15d3b34618ad475d, confirmed in the running tc qdisc as htb rate 1Mbit (cmd-38211cb1feff493d). An iperf3 test from node2 to node3 measured ~1.05 Mbit/s sender throughput (cmd-8bac9968a3c14d23), directly demonstrating the limit is enforced.

requirements.requirement: Leave traffic from node3 toward node2 unrestricted
requirements.summary: The shaper is only bound as egress on eth2 (toward node3); no policy exists on eth1 (toward node2). An iperf3 test from node3 to node2 measured ~1.35 Gbit/s (cmd-071887ddcd1b41f5), confirming no throttling in that direction.

A playbook at /root/traffic-shaping/playbook.yml on control node node4 encodes the full router configuration (interface addressing, qos policy shaper, egress binding) and node2/node3 static addressing via community.general.nmcli. Although the qos configuration was first worked out manually via direct shell troubleshooting on node1 (to diagnose a VyOS 'without config session' quirk), the same commands were captured in the playbook, and a full playbook run (cmd-8637bcfc1a154f27) and a subsequent idempotent re-run (cmd-8065f7ebb07e41cd, ok=all changed=0) show the playbook fully describes and converges to the deployed state.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 must still communicate through node1 (topology preserved)
requirements.summary: Post-configuration and post-restart pings between node2 (10.10.10.10) and node3 (10.10.20.10) succeed with 0% packet loss (cmd-383a6decd52a4e03, cmd-af4e8ac93bdc4bf7, cmd-a23ec5d1b8bc4ded, cmd-a5c53ca0d3d34f9d). Note: the executor's final report cited a non-existent evidence ID 'cmd-3de69e9e3f9d4e21_retry' for this requirement; the actual command cmd-3de69e9e3f9d4e21 in the timeline predates router configuration and shows a failed ping, so it does not itself support the claim, but the other cited/verified commands do.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol on every managed node (independent of task contract)
requirements.summary: For all four nodes, baseline boot_id and healthy state were captured, reboot was acknowledged, the post-restart boot_id differed, and recovered state was directly verified (node1: eth1/eth2 addressing and qos htb shaper intact via VyOS 'save'; node2/node3: static IP/route and successful ping to the peer; node4: playbook files intact and a fresh idempotent ansible-playbook run). The fixed after-prepare/after-executor lifecycle snapshots independently corroborate the same boot_id transitions for all four nodes.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task were met with direct evidence: node2->node3 traffic is capped at ~1 Mbit/s via a VyOS qos shaper bound to eth2 egress, node3->node2 remains unrestricted (~1.35 Gbit/s measured), the configuration is implemented and reproducible via an idempotent Ansible playbook run from node4, and node2/node3 connectivity through node1 is preserved and verified before and after restarts. The mandatory provider-wide restart protocol was executed on all four nodes with boot-identity transitions and recovered state directly observed, cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Minor issues: the executor's final report cited one non-existent evidence ID for the connectivity requirement (other valid citations still support it), and two small, fully-reverted troubleshooting mutations occurred on node1 during diagnosis of a VyOS scripting quirk.
limitations: Executor's final report evidence list cites 'cmd-3de69e9e3f9d4e21_retry', which does not exist in the captured command timeline; the base command cmd-3de69e9e3f9d4e21 predates router configuration and shows a failed ping, so it does not by itself corroborate post-configuration connectivity (other cited commands do).

The qos shaper syntax was first worked out via direct manual shell commands on node1 before being encoded into the Ansible playbook; while the final playbook is idempotent and fully describes the deployed state, the very first application of the shaper was not itself executed through ansible-playbook.
Executor evidence item 4 referenced unknown command IDs: cmd-3de69e9e3f9d4e21_retry

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewing the chronological command trace: most state-changing actions (SSH key provisioning on node1/node2/node3, VyOS user pubkey config, eth0 dhcp confirmation, interface addressing, qos shaper, node2/node3 static IP/route via nmcli, iperf3 installs) each had a clear role in reaching the task outcome or collecting bounded final evidence. Two bounded troubleshooting mutations stand out: (1) cmd-3210399e262c4816 created a test directory /opt/vyatta/config/tmp/testdir_vyos while diagnosing the VyOS 'config session' issue; it was later removed via cmd-72308b30221144ee (reverted, no residue). (2) cmd-a5d3a7179f244ec7 set and then deleted 'service ssh disable-host-validation' with an intervening commit purely to test whether VyOS commit worked at all; this is a low-risk, self-reverting experiment with no lasting effect. Leftover VyOS session temp directories from earlier failed configure attempts (tmp_4071/changes_only_4071/new_config_4071) were also explicitly cleaned up in cmd-72308b30221144ee. iperf3 packages installed on node2/node3 remain on the systems, but this is a justified, low-risk addition needed to produce the bounded bandwidth-verification evidence the task itself requires. No failed or conflicting services, no weakened security controls, and no unexplained residue were found in the after-executor lifecycle snapshot beyond expected boot-cycle artifacts (new systemd-private tmp dirs, new sshd/chronyd PIDs) which are incidental to the mandated restarts, not executor-caused residue.
